words: A scientist who studies fossils to learn about ancient life. Paleontologists are fossil detectives.
To study data carefully, looking for patterns and details that help explain something.
Information collected in a science investigation: measurements, observations, drawings, and descriptions. Fossils are data.
A careful conclusion you reach by putting together what you observe and what you already know.
Tiny pieces of rock, sand, or mud that settle in layers over time and can turn into rock.
From a very long time ago, millions of years before today.

parts.title: Observation Comes First
parts.html:
Before a paleontologist explains anything, she looks carefully and writes down exactly what she sees. That is called recording data.

An observation is only what your senses tell you. "The fossil has ridges" is an observation. "It came from a shellfish" is already an inference.

parts.title: From Data to Inference
parts.html:
Next, scientists analyze the data. They ask: What patterns do I see? What does this remind me of in living things today?

A strong inference names the clue that supports it. "This animal may have eaten plants because its teeth are flat and wide" is strong. "This animal looked weird" is not.

parts.title: The Rock Is Data, Too
parts.html:
For a fossil to form, a living thing must be buried quickly in sediment: sand, mud, or volcanic ash. Over millions of years, the sediment hardens into rock.

The kind of rock is a clue. Dark mudstone often forms in wet, swampy places. Pale limestone can form in calm, shallow water. Gray-green shale forms in quiet water where fine mud settles.

compare.title: Where can a footprint last?
compare.look: Two real footprints, each on a lit specimen tray. One was pressed into rock long ago. The other was made in mud this year. Under the trays are two kinds of ground for a model test: wet mud and dry sand.

trays.alt: A deep three-toed dinosaur footprint in red rock, with a coin beside it
trays.label: Specimen A

trays.alt: A trail of small three-toed bird footprints in gray mud, next to green marsh plants
trays.label: Specimen B

ask.q: Which footprint is old, pressed into hard rock?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen A is pressed into hard red rock. The coin shows how big it is.
ask.miss: Look closely. Which one is in hard rock, not soft mud?

ask.q: Which footprints were made by birds walking in mud?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen B shows a trail of small bird prints in soft, wet mud.
ask.miss: Look again. Which tray shows a trail of small prints in soft mud?

compare.testDo: Drag the wet mud under one tray and the dry sand under the other, or tap each one, then tap a tray. Press Step down. Then swap them and press it again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. It shows why footprints last best in soft, wet mud. A real track also needs new mud to cover it before wind and rain wear it away.

Amud.text: The big three-toed foot sank in. Every toe stayed sharp in the wet mud.

Asand.text: The dry sand slid back in. The big print fell apart.

Bmud.text: The bird's thin toes left a clean print in the wet mud.

Bsand.text: Dry sand poured into the tiny print. You can barely see it.

compare.frame: This ___ has ___, so I think the ground was ___.
compare.claimMid: so I think the ground was

curator.A: Sharp toe marks → the ground was soft, wet mud. Specimen A is a real dinosaur track in red rock. The mud it was pressed into later turned to stone, with the footprint still in it.
curator.B: Sharp toe marks → soft, wet mud. Specimen B shows fresh bird tracks in marsh mud. Many dinosaur tracks look a lot like bird tracks. Scientists have found that birds came from dinosaurs.

compare.missFeat: Look at the footprint on {label} again. Can you see the toes?
compare.missClaim: Think about your test. Which ground kept the print?
compare.done: Footprints last in soft, wet ground. So a footprint in mudstone is evidence that the ground there was once wet mud.

after.kicker: 🎬 Behind the scenes · Even cracks turn to stone
after.alt: A slab of red rock covered with a pattern of cracks, like dried mud
after.html: These cracks formed when wet mud dried out in the sun, more than a billion years ago, in what is now Glacier National Park, Montana. New mud covered them, and they turned to stone. The rock itself is evidence: this place was wet, and then it dried out.

wall.title: Dig down through Site 7-B
wall.look: A cutaway (a slice) of the hillside at Site 7-B. It is a model of the three rock layers in Dr. Reyes's field data. Each layer has its own kind of rock and its own fossils. The brass dial on the left is a depth gauge. It shows how deep you are.
wall.do: First, make a prediction. Then brush the glowing layer: drag across it (or tap it again and again) until the fossil shows.

predict.q: Can the ROCK around a fossil tell you anything, or only the fossil?
options: the rock is a clue too
The rock is a clue too
predict.answer: the rock is a clue too
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's dig and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted the rock is a clue too. The evidence agrees: in every layer, the rock told you about the place.
predict.change: You predicted only the fossil tells us. The evidence changed that idea: in every layer, the rock told you about the place too.

wall.skyAlt: A dry, bare hillside of striped rock today
wall.locked: Clear the layer above first. It sits on top, so you reach it first.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going deeper, and farther back in time. Brush Layer {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line on the hillside. The deepest layer formed first, so it is the oldest. The top layer is the newest.
wall.rule: At Site 7-B, the place changed over time. In each layer, the fossils AND the rock tell what the place was like then.

layers.name: Layer 1 · 80 cm
layers.alt: A spiral shell fossil in pale gray limestone
layers.ask: Look at Layer 1. Read the rock AND the fossil. What was this place like?
layers.clue: Rock: pale gray limestone, smooth and fine. It forms in calm, shallow water. Fossil: a spiral shell (Find 1).
layers.ok: Yes! The rock and the shell both point to a calm, shallow sea.

miss.1: A swamp makes dark mud, but this rock is pale limestone. Read the rock clue again.
miss.2: Look at the clue: there's a shell, not a fish, and the rock is limestone from a calm, shallow sea.

layers.envAlt: Clear, shallow sea water over sand and sea plants
layers.envCap: Long ago here: a calm, shallow sea · Photo: a shallow sea today, Florida Keys

layers.name: Layer 2 · 140 cm
layers.ask: Now Layer 2. Read the rock AND the fossils. What was this place like?
layers.clue: Rock: dark mudstone, almost black. Dark rock like this forms in a wet place, like a swamp or a still lake bottom. Fossils: a fern and two footprints (Finds 2 and 3).
layers.ok: Yes! Dark mud, a fern, and footprints point to a wet, muddy swamp.

miss.0: Pale limestone forms in calm water, but this rock is dark mudstone. And ferns grow on wet land.
miss.2: Ferns don't grow underwater, and footprints need ground to walk on. Read the clue again.

layers.envAlt: Tall cypress trees standing in dark swamp water
layers.envCap: Long ago here: a wet, muddy swamp · Photo: Big Cypress Swamp, Florida, today

layers.name: Layer 3 · 210 cm
layers.alt: Two fossil fish skeletons in pale rock
layers.ask: Last one: Layer 3, the deepest. Read the rock AND the fossils. What was this place like?
layers.clue: Rock: gray-green shale in thin, flat layers. It forms in quiet water where fine mud settles. Fossils: a whole fish skeleton and a sharp tooth (Finds 4 and 5).
layers.ok: Yes! Thin layers of fine mud and a whole fish point to quiet water, like a lake.

miss.0: Look at the rock: thin, flat shale, not pale limestone. And here there's a whole fish. Which choice has fish?
miss.1: The swamp layer had a fern and footprints. Here, thin shale and a whole fish point to open, quiet water.

layers.envAlt: A calm lake with a cypress tree at the shore
layers.envCap: Long ago here: quiet water with fish · Photo: Lake Iamonia, Florida, today

mix.q: The fern (Find 2) and the fish (Find 4) came from the same hillside. Did they live there at the same time?

options.t: Yes. They were found at the same site, so they lived together.
options.miss: Same site, but not the same layer. The fish is 70 cm deeper, in a different rock. Deeper layers formed first.

options.t: No. They are in different layers, so they lived at different times. The place changed.
options.ok: Yes! First, quiet water with fish covered this spot. Much later, it became a swamp with ferns. The PLACE changed over time.

wow.title: The oldest fossils on Earth
wow.alt: Dark, rounded rock-like mounds in clear, shallow sea water
wow.caption: Living stromatolites at Shark Bay, Western Australia, today.
wow.html:
These lumpy mounds are called stromatolites. Tiny living things, too small to see, build them layer by layer in shallow sea water.

Scientists think fossils of mounds like these are among the oldest fossils ever found: about 3.5 billion years old, in rock in Australia. That's long before plants, fish, or dinosaurs.
wow.insetCap: A fossil stromatolite from Wyoming. See its layers?

keyIdea: Scientists observe first and record exact data. Then they make an inference that points back to that data. The rock around a fossil is data too, and more clues that agree make a stronger inference.

det.look: Dr. Reyes's field data: five finds from Site 7-B, each on a slab card with a real fossil photo. Site 7-B is a practice dataset, built like the ones real scientists collect. Under the cards is an evidence chart, a table that holds what you figure out.
det.do: Pick 3 cards, one at a time. For each one, tap a clue you see and pick what it was. Then predict where it lived and watch the past appear. Your answers fill the chart.

clues.t: A spine, fin rays, and a tail

clues.miss: Look again. There are no toes. What long line runs down the middle?

items.alt: A curved, pointed fossil tooth with tiny saw-like edges

clues.t: Saw-like edges, and found 20 cm from a fish

clues.miss: 'Big' is only one clue, and it doesn't tell what the animal ate. Look for clues that work together.
'Looks scary' isn't an observation. What exact shape do you see, and what was it found next to?

quiz.q: A student writes: "This fossil looks like it might be a fish." What did they do wrong?

options.miss: They did look at the fossil. The problem is what they wrote. A strong inference names exactly which observations support it. What features would point to a fish?
Writing it down isn't the problem. A strong inference names exactly which observations support it. What features would point to a fish?

options.t: They jumped to a conclusion without naming specific evidence.
options.ok: 🔬 Exactly! "Looks like" isn't a scientific inference. It needs specific data, like "it has fins, a spine, and a tail, which are features of fish."

quiz.q: A scientist finds a fossil in dark, fine-grained mudstone. What does the type of sediment add to her investigation?

options.t: Nothing. Only the fossil shape matters.
options.miss: The rock around a fossil is data too. What kind of place makes dark, fine mud?

options.t: It is more data. Dark mudstone forms in wet places like swamps.
options.ok: 🪨 Right! The rock itself is data. Dark mudstone is a clue that the place was wet, like a swamp.

options.t: It tells her the fossil is not very old.
options.miss: The color of the rock doesn't tell age. What kind of place makes dark, fine mud?

quiz.q: Which is the strongest, most scientific inference about a tooth fossil?

options.t: "The tooth is curved, serrated (saw-like), and found near bone pieces, so this animal was likely a predator."
options.ok: ⭐ Excellent! It names three specific observations AND connects them to the inference. That's strong scientific evidence.

options.t: "The tooth is big, so this was a dangerous animal."
options.miss: Compare the choices. Which one names the most specific observations AND connects them to the conclusion?

options.t: "This tooth looks like it belongs to a meat eater."
options.miss: "Looks like" doesn't name evidence. Which choice names the most specific observations AND connects them to the conclusion?

partA.title: Observation or inference?
partA.do: Read each one. Pick the best answer, or type your answer.

items.q: "The fossil has ridges that curve from the center toward the outer edge." Is this an observation or an inference?

options.t: An observation. It only describes what you can see.
options.ok: Yes. It describes the ridges and doesn't explain anything.

options.t: An inference. It explains what the animal was.
options.miss: Does it explain anything, or only describe what you see? Read it again.

items.q: "This organism lived in a shallow ocean because it is a shell fossil." Is this an observation or an inference? Is it strong or weak? What would make it stronger?
"The fossil is preserved in dark mudstone with fine grains." Which answer is best?

options.t: An observation. A scientist could infer the place was wet and swampy.
options.ok: Yes. It describes the rock, and dark, fine mud points to a wet, swampy place.

options.t: An inference. It tells us the fossil is very old.
options.miss: Does it describe the rock, or explain something? And does rock color tell age?

options.t: An observation. A scientist could infer the place was a dry desert.
options.miss: It is an observation. But fine, dark mud settles in wet places, not dry deserts.
